topics.title: Why do we need political parties?

concepts.label: Meaning and Components of a Political Party
concepts.cardText: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. They agree on some policies and programmes for the society with a view to promote the collective good, and try to persuade people that their policies are better. Parties reflect fundamental political divisions in a society and involve partisanship. A party has three components: the leaders, the active members and the followers.

concepts.label: Functions of Political Parties
concepts.cardText: Political parties fill political offices and exercise political power. They contest elections; put forward policies and programmes, reducing a vast multitude of opinions into a few basic positions; play a decisive role in making laws; form and run governments; act as the opposition when they lose; shape public opinion by raising issues and launching movements; and give people access to government machinery and welfare schemes.
concepts.hint: Think about elections, policies, laws, government, opposition, public opinion and access to government.
concepts.probe: What are the various functions that political parties perform in a democracy?
concepts.causeChain: Too many individual opinions for any government -> parties group similar opinions into a few basic positions -> voters choose among these policies -> the government bases its policies on the ruling party's line

causeLinks.criterion: Explains that because no government can handle a large variety of views, parties group similar opinions into a few basic positions that voters can choose from.

keyPoints.text: Parties contest elections. In most democracies, elections are fought mainly among the candidates put up by political parties. In some countries, such as the USA, members and supporters of a party choose its candidates; in countries like India, top party leaders choose candidates.
keyPoints.followUp: What part do parties play in elections, and who decides whom they put up?

checks.criterion: Names contesting elections (putting up candidates) as a function of parties.
Mentions that in the USA party members and supporters choose candidates, while in India top party leaders choose them.

keyPoints.text: Parties put forward different policies and programmes and the voters choose from them. No government can handle a large variety of views, so a party reduces a vast multitude of opinions into a few basic positions which it supports. A government is expected to base its policies on the line taken by the ruling party.
keyPoints.followUp: How do parties help voters choose among so many different opinions?

checks.criterion: Names putting forward policies and programmes as a function, reducing many opinions into a few basic positions.

keyPoints.text: Parties play a decisive role in making laws: most members of the legislature belong to a party and go by the direction of the party leadership. Parties form and run governments: they recruit leaders, train them and make them ministers. Parties that lose play the role of opposition, voicing different views and criticising the government for its failures or wrong policies.
keyPoints.followUp: What role do parties play in the legislature and in running or opposing governments?

checks.criterion: Names making laws as a function, since legislators go by the direction of the party leadership.

keyPoints.text: Parties shape public opinion: they raise and highlight issues, and sometimes launch movements for the resolution of problems faced by people. Parties provide people access to government machinery and welfare schemes: for an ordinary citizen it is easy to approach a local party leader than a government officer.
keyPoints.followUp: How do parties shape what people think, and how do they help ordinary citizens reach the government?

checks.criterion: Names shaping public opinion (raising issues, launching movements) as a function.

concepts.label: Necessity of Political Parties
concepts.cardText: Without parties, every candidate would be independent, so no one could promise major policy changes, and no one would be responsible for how the country is run. Even in non-party panchayat elections, villages split into factions that put up 'panels' of candidates, which is exactly what a party does. The rise of parties is directly linked to representative democracy: large societies need an agency to gather views, form a responsible government, and support or restrain it. Parties are a necessary condition for a democracy.
concepts.hint: Imagine an election where every candidate is independent. Who would be responsible for running the country?
concepts.probe: Why can modern democracies not exist without political parties?
concepts.causeChain: Large, complex societies need representative democracy -> need an agency to gather views, bring representatives together and form a responsible government -> political parties fulfil these needs -> parties are a necessary condition for democracy

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the needs of large representative democracies (gathering views, forming a responsible government) to parties being a necessary condition for democracy.

keyPoints.text: Imagine a situation without parties. Every candidate in the elections will be independent. So no one will be able to make any promises to the people about any major policy changes. Elected representatives will be accountable to their constituency, but no one will be responsible for how the country will be run.
keyPoints.followUp: What would elections and government be like if there were no parties?

checks.criterion: Explains that without parties every candidate would be independent, no one could promise major policy changes, or no one would be responsible for how the country is run.

keyPoints.text: In non-party based elections to the panchayat in many states, the village gets split into more than one faction, each of which puts up a 'panel' of its candidates. This is exactly what the party does. That is the reason we find political parties in almost all countries of the world.

checks.criterion: Gives the example of non-party panchayat elections where villages split into factions that put up panels of candidates, which is what parties do.

keyPoints.text: The rise of political parties is directly linked to the emergence of representative democracies. Large societies need representative democracy. They needed some agency to gather different views and present these to the government, to bring representatives together so that a responsible government could be formed, and to support or restrain the government. Political parties fulfill these needs. Parties are a necessary condition for a democracy.

topics.title: How many parties should we have?

concepts.label: One-Party, Two-Party and Multiparty Systems
concepts.cardText: In a one-party system, only one party is allowed to control and run the government, as in China; this is not a democratic option, since a democracy must allow at least two parties a fair chance to come to power. In a two-party system, power usually changes between two main parties, as in the USA and the UK. In a multiparty system, as in India, more than two parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power, often through coalitions, alliances or fronts. It can seem messy and unstable, but lets a variety of interests be represented.
concepts.hint: Compare China, the USA and India. How many parties have a real chance of forming the government?
concepts.probe: What are one-party, two-party and multiparty systems? Why is a one-party system not a democratic option?
concepts.causeChain: One party allowed to rule -> no free competition for power -> not a democratic option; several parties with a real chance -> coalitions and alliances -> messy and unstable, but varied interests get represented

causeLinks.criterion: Explains that a one-party system is not democratic because democracy requires at least two parties with a fair chance to come to power.

keyPoints.text: In some countries, only one party is allowed to control and run the government. These are called one-party systems. In China, only the Communist Party is allowed to rule. We cannot consider one-party system as a good option because this is not a democratic option. Any democratic system must allow at least two parties to compete in elections and provide a fair chance for the competing parties to come to power.
keyPoints.followUp: What is a one-party system, and why is it not considered democratic?

checks.criterion: Describes a one-party system, where only one party is allowed to control and run the government (for example China).

keyPoints.text: In some countries, power usually changes between two main parties. Several other parties may exist, but only the two main parties have a serious chance of winning majority of seats to form government. Such a party system is called two-party system. The United States of America and the United Kingdom are examples of two-party system.
keyPoints.followUp: What is a two-party system? Give an example of a country that has one.

checks.criterion: Describes a two-party system, where power usually changes between two main parties (for example the USA or the UK).

keyPoints.text: If several parties compete for power, and more than two parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power either on their own strength or in alliance with others, we call it a multiparty system. India has a multiparty system. When several parties join hands for contesting elections and winning power, it is called an alliance or a front, such as the National Democratic Alliance, the United Progressive Alliance and the Left Front in 2004. The multiparty system often appears very messy and leads to political instability, but it allows a variety of interests and opinions to enjoy political representation.
keyPoints.followUp: What is a multiparty system, and what are its strengths and weaknesses?

checks.criterion: Describes a multiparty system, where more than two parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power on their own or in alliance (for example India).

concepts.label: Why a Party System Cannot Be Chosen
concepts.cardText: Which party system is better is not a very good question. A party system is not something any country can choose. It evolves over a long time, depending on the nature of society, its social and regional divisions, its history of politics and its system of elections. India evolved a multiparty system because its social and geographical diversity is not easily absorbed by two or even three parties. No system is ideal for all countries and all situations.

concepts.label: Popular Participation in Political Parties
concepts.cardText: It is often said that parties face a crisis because citizens are indifferent to them. Surveys show this is only partly true for India. Political parties do not enjoy much trust in South Asia, and are among the least trusted institutions all over the world. Yet participation in party activities is fairly high: the proportion of party members is higher in India than in many advanced countries like Canada, Japan, Spain and South Korea, and membership and feeling close to a party have gone up.

concepts.label: Recognised National and State Parties
concepts.cardText: Federal democracies have parties present in only one federal unit and parties present in several or all units. Every party must register with the Election Commission, which gives large, established parties special facilities, such as a unique election symbol; these are 'recognised political parties'. A party with at least six per cent of the votes in a State Assembly election and at least two seats is a State party. A party with at least six per cent of the votes in Lok Sabha or Assembly elections in four States and at least four Lok Sabha seats is a national party.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects meeting the Election Commission's vote and seat criteria to a party being recognised and getting a unique election symbol.

keyPoints.text: Democracies that follow a federal system tend to have two kinds of parties: parties present in only one of the federal units and parties present in several or all units. Country-wide parties are called 'national parties'; their units in various states follow the same policies, programmes and strategy decided at the national level.

These parties are given a unique symbol: only the official candidates of that party can use that election symbol. These parties are called 'recognised political parties'.

A party that secures at least six per cent of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four States and wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha is recognised as a national party.

concepts.label: National Parties of India
concepts.cardText: There are six recognised national parties (Election Commission notification, 2023): the Aam Aadmi Party (formed 2012, after the anti-corruption movement), the Bahujan Samaj Party (formed 1984 under Kanshi Ram, for the bahujan samaj), the Bharatiya Janata Party (founded 1980, inspired by integral humanism and Antyodaya, leads the NDA), the Communist Party of India (Marxist) (founded 1964, Marxism-Leninism), the Indian National Congress (founded 1885, centrist, led the UPA from 2004 to 2019) and the National People's Party (formed 2013, first national party from the North East).

concepts.label: State Parties
concepts.cardText: Most of the major parties are classified as 'State parties', commonly called regional parties. They need not be regional in ideology: some, like the Samajwadi Party and Rashtriya Janata Dal, have national-level organisations, while others, like the Biju Janata Dal, Sikkim Democratic Front and Mizo National Front, are conscious about their State identity. Their number and strength have grown, making Parliament more diverse. No national party won a Lok Sabha majority on its own until 2014, so national parties formed alliances with State parties. This has strengthened federalism and democracy.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects national parties needing alliances with State parties to the strengthening of federalism and democracy.

keyPoints.text: Most of the major parties of the country are classified by the Election Commission as 'State parties', commonly referred to as regional parties. Yet these parties need not be regional in their ideology or outlook. Some, like the Samajwadi Party and Rashtriya Janata Dal, have national level political organisation with units in several states. Some, like Biju Janata Dal, Sikkim Democratic Front, Mizo National Front and Telangana Rashtra Samithi, are conscious about their State identity.

concepts.label: Four Challenges to Political Parties
concepts.cardText: Popular dissatisfaction with parties focuses on four problem areas. First, lack of internal democracy: power is concentrated in one or few leaders, and parties keep no membership registers and hold no regular internal elections. Second, dynastic succession: top positions are controlled by one family, which is unfair to other members and bad for democracy. Third, the growing role of money and muscle power, especially during elections. Fourth, parties often do not offer a meaningful choice, as ideological differences between them have declined.
concepts.hint: Think of four problems: internal democracy, family control, money and muscle, and choice.
concepts.probe: What are the various challenges faced by political parties?
concepts.causeChain: Power concentrated in a few leaders, no open procedures -> ordinary workers cannot rise -> leaders favour family members (dynastic succession); parties focused only on winning -> use short-cuts -> money and muscle power

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the lack of open and transparent procedures inside parties to dynastic succession, since leaders can favour people close to them.

keyPoints.text: The first challenge is lack of internal democracy within parties. There is a tendency towards the concentration of power in one or few leaders at the top. Parties do not keep membership registers, do not hold organisational meetings, and do not conduct internal elections regularly. Personal loyalty to the leader becomes more important than loyalty to party principles.
keyPoints.followUp: What is the first challenge parties face in how they are run inside?

checks.criterion: Names lack of internal democracy as a challenge: power concentrated in one or few leaders, no membership registers, meetings or regular internal elections.

keyPoints.text: The second challenge of dynastic succession is related to the first. Since most parties do not practice open and transparent procedures, there are very few ways for an ordinary worker to rise to the top. In many parties, the top positions are always controlled by members of one family. This is unfair to other members, and bad for democracy, since people who do not have adequate experience or popular support come to occupy positions of power.
keyPoints.followUp: How do top positions in many parties get passed on, and why is that a problem?

checks.criterion: Names dynastic succession as a challenge: top positions controlled by members of one family, unfair to other members and bad for democracy.

keyPoints.text: The third challenge is about the growing role of money and muscle power in parties, especially during elections. Parties tend to nominate candidates who have or can raise lots of money. Rich people and companies who give funds tend to have influence on the policies and decisions of the party. In some cases, parties support criminals who can win elections.
keyPoints.followUp: What role do money and force play in parties, especially at election time?

checks.criterion: Names the growing role of money and muscle power as a challenge: rich candidates, influence of funders, or support for criminals who can win.

keyPoints.text: The fourth challenge is that very often parties do not seem to offer a meaningful choice to the voters. There has been a decline in the ideological differences among parties: the difference between the Labour Party and the Conservative Party in Britain is very little, and in India the differences among major parties on economic policies have reduced. Sometimes the same set of leaders keep shifting from one party to another.
keyPoints.followUp: Why do voters sometimes feel that parties offer them no real choice?

concepts.label: Recent Efforts to Reform Parties
concepts.cardText: Three recent efforts: the Constitution was amended so that an MLA or MP who changes parties loses the seat, which brought defection down but made dissent harder; a Supreme Court order made it mandatory for candidates to file an affidavit giving details of property and pending criminal cases, though there is no system to check it; and an Election Commission order requires parties to hold organisational elections and file income tax returns, though sometimes it is a mere formality.
concepts.hint: Think of the anti-defection amendment, the Supreme Court's affidavit order, and the Election Commission's order.
concepts.probe: What efforts have been made in India to reform political parties, and what are their limits?
concepts.causeChain: Elected representatives defecting for ministerial posts or cash -> Constitution amended -> defection falls, but dissent becomes harder; influence of money and criminals -> affidavits on property and criminal cases -> more information, but no check on truth

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the anti-defection amendment (an MLA or MP who changes parties loses the seat) to defection coming down but dissent becoming more difficult.

keyPoints.text: The Constitution was amended to prevent elected MLAs and MPs from changing parties, because many were indulging in defection to become ministers or for cash rewards. Now if any MLA or MP changes parties, he or she will lose the seat in the legislature. This has helped bring defection down, but has made any dissent even more difficult.
keyPoints.followUp: What change was made to stop MLAs and MPs from switching parties, and what was its side effect?

checks.criterion: Explains the anti-defection amendment: an MLA or MP who changes parties loses the seat in the legislature.
Mentions that the law brought defection down but made dissent more difficult.

keyPoints.text: The Supreme Court passed an order to reduce the influence of money and criminals. It is mandatory for every candidate who contests elections to file an affidavit giving details of his property and criminal cases pending against him. This has made a lot of information available to the public, but there is no system to check if the information is true.
keyPoints.followUp: What must every candidate now tell voters before an election, and why?

checks.criterion: Explains the Supreme Court order requiring candidates to file an affidavit giving details of property and pending criminal cases.

keyPoints.text: The Election Commission passed an order making it necessary for political parties to hold their organisational elections and file their income tax returns. The parties have started doing so but sometimes it is mere formality.

checks.criterion: Mentions the Election Commission order requiring parties to hold organisational elections and file income tax returns.

concepts.label: Suggested Reforms and the Role of Citizens
concepts.cardText: Suggested reforms include a law to regulate parties' internal affairs (membership registers, an independent authority for disputes, open elections to top posts); giving about one-third of tickets to women; and state funding of elections. But we must be careful about legal solutions: over-regulation can be counter-productive, and parties will not pass laws they do not like. Parties can also be reformed through people's pressure, by petitions, publicity and agitations, and by citizens who want reform joining parties. The problem of bad politics can be solved by more and better politics.
concepts.hint: Besides new laws, what can ordinary citizens do to reform parties?
concepts.probe: Suggest some reforms to strengthen political parties. Why are laws alone not enough?
concepts.causeChain: Laws alone risk over-regulation and parties will not pass laws they dislike -> people's pressure (petitions, publicity, agitations) and joining parties -> parties take reform seriously -> more and better politics

causeLinks.criterion: Explains that because legal solutions have limits, people's pressure and participation are needed to make parties reform.

keyPoints.text: Suggestions to reform parties: a law to regulate the internal affairs of political parties (a register of members, an independent authority to judge party disputes, open elections to the highest posts); making it mandatory to give about one-third of tickets to women, with a quota for women in decision-making bodies; and state funding of elections, in kind or in cash based on votes secured in the last election.
keyPoints.followUp: Suggest some changes in the law that could improve how political parties work.

Suggests giving about one-third of tickets to women candidates, or a quota for women in parties' decision-making bodies.
Suggests state funding of elections, in kind (petrol, paper, telephone) or in cash based on votes.

keyPoints.text: We must be very careful about legal solutions to political problems. Over-regulation of political parties can be counter-productive; it would force all parties to find ways to cheat the law. Besides, political parties will not agree to pass a law that they do not like.

checks.criterion: Explains the limits of legal solutions: over-regulation can be counter-productive and parties will not pass laws they do not like.

keyPoints.text: People can put pressure on political parties through petitions, publicity and agitations; ordinary citizens, pressure groups and movements and the media can play an important role. Political parties can also improve if those who want this join political parties. The quality of democracy depends on the degree of public participation. The problem of bad politics can be solved by more and better politics.
keyPoints.followUp: Apart from laws, how can ordinary citizens push parties to improve?

checks.criterion: Explains that people can pressure parties through petitions, publicity and agitations (citizens, pressure groups, movements and the media).
Explains that parties can improve if those who want reform join them; the problem of bad politics can be solved by more and better politics.
